client: I've been really struggling to focus on my schoolwork since my grandmother passed away last month. I keep zoning out during lectures and putting off assignments, which just makes me feel more guilty on top of the sadness. Part of me wonders if talking about it will even help - the pain feels too deep to just "talk through."
therapist: I hear how deeply this loss is affecting you, both emotionally and in your daily life. It makes complete sense that concentrating feels difficult when you're carrying this weight of grief. Would it feel okay to explore how the guilt and sadness show up for you when you try to focus on schoolwork?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It's like whenever I open my textbook, I immediately remember how my grandma used to check on me while I studied. Then I feel guilty for not visiting her more before she passed. The sadness hits so hard that I just close my books and scroll on my phone to numb it. But then I feel even worse for procrastinating.
therapist: Your words paint such a vivid picture of that painful moment when memories of your grandmother surface while studying. I notice your voice quickens when describing this cycle - almost like the emotions come on so fast that scrolling becomes an automatic escape. Could we slow down together and look at what happens right before you reach for your phone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: It's like this tightness in my chest starts building when I see my homework reminders. Then I picture her smiling face from when she'd bring me snacks while I studied, and suddenly my eyes sting with tears. I grab my phone because the physical pain of sadness feels too intense to sit with - but I'm not sure avoiding it is helping either.
therapist: You're describing such a powerful physical and emotional experience - that tightness, the sting of tears - with such clarity. It sounds like you're beginning to notice that while the phone gives temporary relief, it might actually be keeping you from processing these important memories of your grandmother. Would it feel helpful to explore other ways you might sit with these feelings when they arise?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I don't know... the idea of sitting with those feelings sounds terrifying. What if I just start crying and can't stop? At least when I scroll I can distract myself until the wave passes. But part of me knows you're right - it's not really helping long term.
therapist: I hear that real fear about being overwhelmed by your emotions - there's such wisdom in recognizing both the short-term relief of scrolling and your sense that it's not serving you well long-term. What comes up for you when you imagine trying something different, like setting a timer for just two minutes to acknowledge the grief before deciding whether to reach for your phone?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Two minutes sounds manageable, but I'm worried I'll just spend that time beating myself up about not studying. And what if the sadness feels even worse when I actually pay attention to it? I don't want to completely fall apart when I have deadlines coming up.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding two important concerns here - the fear that focusing on the grief might intensify it, and the very real pressure of your upcoming deadlines. That's a really difficult balance to navigate. What would it be like to approach those two minutes with curiosity rather than judgment, simply noticing what emotions come up without trying to change them?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I could try being curious instead of critical... but it's hard to imagine. My mind automatically jumps to "you should be studying" when I feel sad. Maybe if I wrote down what comes up during those two minutes instead of just thinking it? Though that still feels like wasted study time.
therapist: I hear that shift in your thinking - from automatic self-criticism to considering writing things down instead. That's a really meaningful step. Your voice softened a bit as you explored this idea - does part of you recognize that honoring your grief might actually create more space for studying in the long run?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I never thought about it that way... that making space for grief could help me focus better later. It's just so counterintuitive because right now it feels like emotions and schoolwork are in constant competition. But I do see how all this avoidance is draining my energy even more.
therapist: It sounds like you're beginning to see how honoring your emotions might actually create more energy in the long run, even though it feels difficult right now. Would it feel helpful to explore together how you might create small moments of emotional space without letting it completely derail your schoolwork?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, maybe... but I'm still worried about losing control if I open that door even a little. Like if I let myself cry for five minutes, what if I can't stop and then I'm a mess for my next class? I know logically that emotions aren't actually dangerous, but they feel so overwhelming right now.
therapist: It sounds like there's a real tension between knowing intellectually that emotions aren't dangerous and the fear that letting them in might feel too overwhelming. What would it be like to start with something smaller than crying - maybe just noticing where in your body you feel the grief most intensely for 30 seconds?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: 30 seconds seems so short it almost feels silly, but I guess that's why it's less scary. I notice it mostly in my throat - this lump that makes it hard to swallow when I think about her. But what if even that small acknowledgment makes the feeling grow instead of helping?
therapist: You're being so thoughtful about this balance - willing to try something small while still noticing that worry about the feelings growing. That lump in your throat tells me how physically present your grief is. What if we viewed these 30 seconds not as a way to "help" the feeling, but simply as practice in noticing it with kindness?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: That makes sense, but I still worry that noticing it with kindness will somehow make the sadness stronger. Like if I'm gentle with myself about missing her, it'll just make the loss feel more real. But I can see how fighting it constantly is exhausting too.
therapist: It sounds like you're holding two important truths here - the fear that acknowledging your sadness might make it feel more real, and the recognition that constantly fighting it is exhausting. That softness in your voice tells me how tender this topic feels for you. What would it be like to experiment with noticing the sadness with kindness for just those 30 seconds, then checking in with yourself to see if it truly made things worse?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech
